decisions.rationale: The passage reports only within-group change (a significant 1RM decrease in VES, p=0.004) and training-vs-nontraining contrasts; no VES-vs-PLB between-group comparison is given, and neither group underwent the training program, so a 'no detectable between-group difference in training adaptation' claim cannot be verified.

The quote shows both PLB+RT and VES+RT increased 1RM versus their non-training counterparts but reports no direct VES+RT vs PLB+RT statistic; with a large significant time×group interaction present, the passage is insufficient to confirm absence of a between-group difference.
Passage states the supplemented (AS) group had higher increases in arm lean mass (0.96 vs 0.59 kg; P=.003) than placebo, directly supporting a larger adaptation in the supplemented group.
Skeletal muscle mass index increased more in AS than PLA (0.71 vs 0.42 kg/m², P=.004), supporting a larger muscle-mass adaptation with supplementation.
Handgrip strength gains were greater in AS than PLA (3.66 vs 1.16 kg, P=.047), supporting an increased strength adaptation with supplementation.
Knee extension strength gains were greater in AS than PLA (2.28 vs 1.02 kg, P<.001), supporting an increased strength adaptation.

The quote reports only the effect of aerobic training itself (increase in VO2 TVE, no change in VO2max); it contains no comparison of a supplemented trained group against a placebo/no-supplement trained control, so the supplement-related direction cannot be verified.

The passage describes a training effect on VO2 TVE without any supplemented-vs-control training comparison; it cannot support an 'increase' in adaptation attributable to supplementation relative to the defined comparator.

Both exercise-only (E) and exercise+vitamin E (EV) groups shortened P3 latency, and the authors conclude the shortening was due to exercise 'instead of vitamin E usage', supporting no added supplement effect versus the training-only comparator.
Peak-to-peak amplitudes were unaltered in all groups, consistent with no detectable between-group difference in this endpoint.
The passage explicitly states neither exercise nor vitamin E altered plasma TAC, supporting no between-group difference.
Passage states supplementation produced no statistical difference in aerobic capacity between supplement and placebo groups at season's end.
Passage states no statistical difference in strength between S and PL groups at the end of the season.
Passage states no statistical difference in speed between S and PL groups, supporting no effect on sprint/power performance.

The quote reports a significant decrease in creatine kinase in 'group 1' without identifying group 1 as the supplemented arm or the placebo comparator, so the direction relative to placebo cannot be confirmed from this passage.
GPx1 declined in both vitamin C and E and placebo groups 'with no effects of supplementation', supporting no between-group difference.
Passage states no changes in muscle mnSOD levels, consistent with no detectable between-group difference.
Passage states no changes in muscle GSH levels, consistent with no between-group difference.
αB-crystallin decreased similarly in both groups 'with no effects of supplementation', supporting no effect.
HSP27 decreased in both groups with explicitly no effects of supplementation, supporting no between-group difference.
Uric acid fell significantly in the vitamin C and E group (−24%) compared with placebo (+6%; P<0.001), supporting a decrease relative to placebo.
Plasma GSH increased in both groups with no effect of supplementation, supporting no between-group difference.
TAS did not change after training or supplementation, supporting no between-group difference.
A statistically significant group×time interaction is reported without any indication of direction or which group changed, so a 'decrease' relative to placebo cannot be verified.
The primary endurance outcome Qend showed no additional increase in the antioxidant group (p=0.56), supporting no detectable difference versus placebo.
A significant between-group difference in QMVC in favor of antioxidant supplementation (p<0.001) supports a larger strength adaptation than placebo.
No significant VO2max changes in either group indicates no differential aerobic adaptation between supplemented and control arms.
